utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to such -- such matters as: "According to the title of this document is minutes of a meeting between," and it goes on. I don't find it -- I don't find it particularly helpful, but I certainly don't object to its inclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you don't object -- of course, sometimes if the title of a document is: This is a list of people who were paid by Mr. X, Y, or Z, then of course if that's -- if that's the title, the comment does not add much to that, apart from that the witness doesn't contradict that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm in accordance with the Haradinaj position on this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Mr. Di Fazio, I take it that you'd like to tender this, and I do understand we were about to hear whether there were any objections --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Tender -- tender what precisely?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 92 ter statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. My -- yes, that is my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And with due -- of course, we'll duly observe the clarifications made by the Defence, and the April statement is then admitted into evidence. I've checked it now on the e-court. Everything is fine now, Mr. Di Fazio. Thank you for that. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And If Your Honours please, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, Mr. Di Fazio, I sometimes am rather critical about timing and times, but it's only fair to say that this time you did perfectly well in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Three things, if I may. First of all, just a short clarification. I've assumed that Your Honour's last ruling in relation to the 92 ter statement is not to be understood by anybody as a ruling that the documents that are referred to in that statement have yet been the subject of a ruling as to their admission in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, Madam Registrar is uploading them, then -- I'm just talking at this moment about --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The statement itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the statement itself and the annexes which have been blacked by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there are no annexes anymore. No, I take it then tomorrow, Mr. Di Fazio, that -- I take it the Defence will have a closer look at it. I do, however, understand that there seems to be no major problems --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That is essentially correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber, of course, would like to hear as soon as possible if there's any remaining problem with any of these documents which are now put into the system by Madam Registrar and provided with sequential numbers marked for identification, Madam Registrar. Yes. We will then later decide on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. There are one or two documents amongst them which neither emanate from this witness nor are documents upon which he purports to recognise the signature of -- and indeed, are not documents purportedly issued by Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So there are one or two individual items that may need to be weeded out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I suggest the following: That Madam Registrar prints out the list once she has assigned numbers to them, and that we'll then hear in a negative way that -- from the Defence teams that this and this there are objections against, well, let's say, be 167 and -- so that we get the numbers of those objected. We can then -- we then can easily decide what is admitted and we'll hear what the objections would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: With respect, I think that's an excellent idea. Can I suggest, though, just the latter part of what Your Honour has discussed. If the Defence were to indicate to us which particular items they object to being admitted into evidence, that that matter could then be resolved by way of written submission rather than -- rather than discussing it. It might make it simpler and take less time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it depends on whether -- it depends on whether we would still need to receive further information from the witness, which of course the Chamber at this moment can't exclude, but if the parties agree at a certain moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: At the conclusion, perhaps, of his evidence, at the conclusion. Because what I would not like to -- to do is to have to come into court and argue the admissibility of a particular document or another one without being prepared properly for it. Now, if the Defence indicates that, it seems to me it's a more orderly manner, and they would then be entitled to respond to us and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the Defence then informs the Prosecution what are the problematic documents and also tells the Prosecution why they are problematic, then we might save time in court. Anything else at this moment, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wonder whether it makes any sense to start with the cross-examination. I don't think so, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Might we use the time to take stock of the position in terms of planning the remainder of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because I appreciate Your Honour's desire to speak to see how the week evolves, but one of the difficulties is in terms of allocating time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we don't have to keep the witness in the courtroom for that reason. Therefore, Mr. Zyrapi, we'll stop for the day. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. And, Madam Registrar, would that be in the same courtroom? No, most likely in Courtroom II. Yes. We'll continue tomorrow in another courtroom, Courtroom II, and I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, whether you gave it already or you're still about to give it tomorrow. Madam Usher, could you escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tomorrow, part of the day will be spent on the cross-examination of this witness. From what I understand, it will be, well, three and a half hours approximately, altogether there might be some more questions. So that takes the whole of the session of tomorrow, I would say, if there are any additional questions by the Bench, we have to look at the admission of some of the documents, whether there are still some problems. So my estimate is that where usually we have some four hours, a little bit over four hours available, that that would take most, if not all, of the time tomorrow. That would mean that the next witness to be called on Wednesday -- Mr. Di Fazio, next witness is scheduled for how much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I can provide you with an answer in a moment, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Two and a half hours I'm being told to my left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right. I've just seen it's two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two and a half hours. Any idea on how much time cross-examination would take?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, my estimate and having discussed it with colleagues, obviously these things are never quite as reliable as one would hope, but my estimate is that we would be thinking of something between two and a half, three hours in total, and possibly less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In total. So that would make altogether five to five and a half hours. The witness scheduled after that, Mr. Di Fazio, how much time would that witness ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: 3.5, three and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three and a half. That would take how much time for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Something similar, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that would make seven hours. So we would then have remaining 12 and a half -- 12 to 12 and a half hours. We'll not sit on -- and that would be after we had finished the cross-examination of this witness, which means that it's totally impossible to hear before Friday both of these remaining witnesses. Under those circumstances -- but let me just confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has looked at it. If the next witness, where cross-examination could not start immediately after examination-in-chief but only on Thursday, then we would use the remaining time, since there's no possibility for the third witness to finish, either we should keep him here. But I think to start with him on Wednesday in chief and then not have him -- that's perhaps not a good idea. On the same time, the third witness scheduled for this week, there's more time needed for him altogether, it's seven hours. I don't know whether there are some -- I mean, if we have to send one witness home for the time being, then the issue is whether it should be the second one or the third one. And that's something perhaps the parties could briefly consider among themselves. Because I do see that we -- if we would start with the third witness, and let's just assume that that would be somewhere later tomorrow, then we would have a -- an assessed seven hours of testimony to be finished this week. If, however, we would start with the second witness, we have an assessed five and a half -- five to five and a half hours to go. So at the end of the week, the question is whether it's better to have a witness remaining for seven hours or to have a witness remaining for five and a half hours. I don't know -- of course it also depends on preparation. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly. One of the concerns I have -- and I had actually thought whether the problems that we have might be resolved by reversing the order of the witnesses. And in fact, whichever witness comes next, for different reasons in terms of the order of preparation and the late service of material on Friday, we are -- I am going to be in difficulties beginning cross-examination before Thursday morning of either of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, so that wouldn't make any --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So in a sense, I think, and given the amount of material that has to be worked through; if, for example, on Wednesday the evidence-in-chief of that witness took less than the full half-day session, I can certainly assure Your Honours that the additional hour or so is time which will be extremely valuably spent in seeking to ensure that we've mastered the material which we are struggling against the time to get on top of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, is there anything you would like to add to that? There seems to be a clear preference of the Defence not to change the order of appearance of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, I don't think that should occur. I think that might lead to complications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't want to say too much, but the personal circumstances of the two witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just seeking your position as whether or not you would have a clear wish to change it in order to save time within your 125 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, that seems not to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We want to maintain the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber then will hear the examination-in-chief of the second witness scheduled for this week to start, once we have finished the cross-examination of the present witness, and the Defence is allowed to start its cross-examination on Thursday, but is expected to finish that also within the time scheduled so that re-examination and questions of the Judges would be finished so that that witness could return at the end of Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I express on behalf of all Defence counsel our thanks for that flexibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, if there's nothing else, we adjourn until tomorrow, 9.00, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 24th day of April, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.,
